claim: During metaphase, the orientation of the mitotic spindle of mammalian APs dynamically deviates from the apical, ventricular surface of the developing cortical wall.
source: During metaphase, the orientation of the mitotic spindle of mammalian APs dynamically deviates from the apical, ventricular surface of the developing cortical wall (Chenn and McConnell, 1995; Haydar et al., 2003; Roszko et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous studies (Chenn and McConnell, 1995; Haydar et al., 2003; Roszko et al., 2006).

claim: The total amplitude of deviations in neurogenic APs was on average twice as high as in proliferating APs (AP proliferating 15.7 ± 1.4°, AP neurogenic 30.7 ± 4.3°).
source: In neurogenic APs, the total amplitude of deviations was on average twice as high as in proliferating APs (Figure 1G; AP proliferating 15.7 ± 1.4°, AP neurogenic 30.7 ± 4.3°).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental measurements shown in Figure 1G, which presents quantitative data on spindle orientation deviations.

claim: The range of metaphase spindle orientations was consistent with the previously reported cleavage plane orientations of fixed and live mouse APs, which have been observed to be mostly perpendicular to the apical surface.
source: Importantly, the range of metaphase spindle orientations (Figure 1D,E) was consistent with the previously reported cleavage plane orientations of fixed (Kosodo et al., 2004) and live (Konno et al., 2008) mouse APs, which have been observed to be mostly perpendicular to the apical surface.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous studies (Kosodo et al., 2004; Konno et al., 2008) and data shown in Figure 1D,E.

claim: Neurogenic BPs showed deviations of the metaphase plate axis from the apical–basal axis of the developing cortical wall that were even greater than those of neurogenic APs.
source: Compared to proliferating APs, neurogenic BPs showed deviations of the metaphase plate axis from the apical–basal axis of the developing cortical wall that were even greater than those of neurogenic APs (Figure 1C,F; Video 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations shown in Figure 1C,F and Video 3.

claim: The total amplitude of deviations in BPs increased to 38.3 ± 5.6°.
source: The total amplitude of deviations in BPs increased to 38.3 ± 5.6° (Figure 1G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Metaphase spindle orientation variability increases as progenitors become neurogenic.
source: This leads to the conclusion that metaphase spindle orientation variability increases as progenitors become neurogenic.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing increased spindle orientation variability in neurogenic progenitors compared to proliferating ones.

claim: The number of astrals reaching the cell cortex was highest in proliferating APs (21.65 ± 1.07) followed by neurogenic APs (16.70 ± 0.98), and lowest in neurogenic BPs (11.36 ± 0.49).
source: Interestingly, the number of astrals reaching the cell cortex was highest in proliferating APs (Figure 2G; 21.65 ± 1.07) followed by neurogenic APs (16.70 ± 0.98), and lowest in neurogenic BPs (11.36 ± 0.49).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The decrease in astrals was specific to the apical and basal regions.
source: Surprisingly, the decrease in astrals was specific to the apical and basal regions.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental observations comparing different regions of the cell.

claim: The number of astrals reaching the apical or basal region of the cell cortex (apical/basal astrals) was lower in neurogenic than in proliferating APs (neurogenic 7.2 ± 0.36, proliferating 11.8 ± 0.43).
source: The number of astrals reaching the apical or basal region of the cell cortex (apical/basal astrals) was lower in neurogenic than in proliferating APs (Figure 2H; neurogenic 7.2 ± 0.36, proliferating 11.8 ± 0.43).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: The number of astrals reaching the central region of the cell cortex (central astrals) did not change significantly between neurogenic and proliferating APs (neurogenic APs 8.8 ± 0.7, proliferating APs 9.1 ± 0.6).
source: By contrast, the number of astrals reaching the central region of the cell cortex (central astrals) did not change significantly (Figure 2I; neurogenic APs 8.8 ± 0.7, proliferating APs 9.1 ± 0.6).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: A higher abundance of apical/basal astrals increases the stability of spindle orientation.
source: Together with our data on spindle orientation variability (Figure 1), this suggests that a higher abundance of apical/basal astrals increases the stability of spindle orientation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between astral abundance and spindle orientation variability data.

claim: In proliferating APs, basal astrals were more abundant than apical ones (6.7 ± 0.31 vs 5.1 ± 0.25).
source: Surprisingly, in proliferating APs, basal astrals were more abundant than apical ones (Figure 2J, 6.7 ± 0.31 vs 5.1 ± 0.25).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2J.

claim: In neurogenic APs, the numbers of both basal and apical astrals were lower than in proliferating APs, but were not significantly different from each other (basal 3.7 ± 0.2, apical 3.4 ± 0.2).
source: By contrast, in neurogenic APs, the numbers of both basal and apical astrals were lower than in proliferating APs, but were not significantly different from each other (basal 3.7 ± 0.2, apical 3.4 ± 0.2).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data comparing basal and apical astrals in neurogenic APs.

claim: The number of astrals in APs decreased 2.5-fold from early to late neurogenesis, from 15.2 ± 0.4 at E11.5 to 9.4 ± 0.5 at E14.5, and further to 6.2 ± 0.3 at E16.5.
source: Indeed, the number of astrals in APs decreased 2.5-fold from early to late neurogenesis, from 15.2 ± 0.4 at E11.5 to 9.4 ± 0.5 at E14.5, and further to 6.2 ± 0.3 at E16.5 (Figure 3).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the E14.5 neocortex of LGN knock-out (KO) mice, fewer apical/basal astrals were found in APs of homozygous compared to heterozygous mice (homozygous 8.4 ± 0.5, heterozygous 11.2 ± 0.7).
source: Indeed, in the E14.5 neocortex of LGN knock-out (KO) mice (Konno et al., 2008) (Figure 4A–D), fewer apical/basal astrals were found in APs of homozygous compared to heterozygous mice (Figure 4E; homozygous 8.4 ± 0.5, heterozygous 11.2 ± 0.7).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data from LGN KO mice shown in Figure 4E.

claim: No significant reduction was seen in the central astrals in LGN KO mice (homozygous 9.1 ± 0.5, heterozygous 8.9 ± 0.3).
source: By contrast, no significant reduction was seen in the central astrals (Figure 4F; homozygous 9.1 ± 0.5, heterozygous 8.9 ± 0.3, similar to unperturbed APs; Figure 2I).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: APs overexpressing LGN-C showed a significant reduction in apical/basal astrals at E14.5 (7.9 ± 0.5), similar to LGN KO homozygous mouse APs.
source: Consistent with our LGN-KO mouse results, APs overexpressing LGN-C also showed a significant reduction in apical/basal astrals at E14.5 (Figure 4J,K, 7.9 ± 0.5), similar to LGN KO homozygous mouse APs (Figure 4E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4J,K.

claim: APs in the electroporated area that were either non-electroporated or overexpressing LGN-wt had a similar number of apical/basal astrals (11.0 ± 0.6 and 11.2 ± 0.4) as unperturbed or LGN-KO heterozygous APs.
source: By contrast, APs in the electroporated area that were either non-electroporated or overexpressing LGN-wt had a similar number of apical/basal astrals (Figure 4H,I,K, 11.0 ± 0.6 and 11.2 ± 0.4) as unperturbed (Figure 2H) or LGN-KO heterozygous (Figure 4E) APs.
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4H,I,K.

claim: LGN perturbations lead to a reduction specifically in apical/basal astrals, likely through reduced anchoring of astrals to the cell cortex.
source: Together, these results show that LGN perturbations lead to a reduction specifically in apical/basal astrals, likely through reduced anchoring of astrals to the cell cortex.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing selective reduction in apical/basal astrals upon LGN perturbation.

claim: In proliferating APs, cortical LGN increased from the apical to the central region of the cell cortex and remained high in most of the central and basal regions.
source: In proliferating APs, cortical LGN increased from the apical to the central region of the cell cortex and remained high in most of the central and basal regions (Figure 5A,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5A,E.

claim: In neurogenic APs, cortical LGN levels were similar to proliferating APs at the apical and central regions, but markedly lower at the basal region.
source: In neurogenic APs, cortical LGN levels were similar to proliferating APs at the apical and central regions, but markedly lower at the basal region (Figure 5B,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B,E.

claim: Neurogenic APs lose LGN enrichment in the basal region of the cell cortex, which could lead to less anchoring of basal astrals.
source: These data show that neurogenic APs lose LGN enrichment in the basal region of the cell cortex, which could lead to less anchoring of basal astrals.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the observed correlation between LGN distribution and astral abundance.

claim: Cortical LGN levels in BPs were much lower than in APs, distributed more homogeneously over the cell and with only minor cortical enrichments.
source: Furthermore, compared to APs, cortical LGN levels in BPs were much lower, distributed more homogeneously over the cell and with only minor cortical enrichments (Figure 5C,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C,E.

claim: With 30 pM nocodazole for 2.5 hr, the mean number of apical/basal astrals in proliferating APs was reduced to 6.7 ± 0.4, similar to untreated neurogenic APs.
source: Most interestingly, in the presence of 30 pM nocodazole for 2.5 hr, the mean number of apical/basal astrals in proliferating APs was reduced to 6.7 ± 0.4 (Figure 6E), similar to untreated neurogenic APs (Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: With 30 pM nocodazole, neither the number of central astrals in proliferating APs, nor the number of central or apical/basal astrals in neurogenic APs, was reduced.
source: For this, we observed that, first, neither the number of central astrals in proliferating APs, nor the number of central or apical/basal astrals in neurogenic APs, was reduced with 30 pM nocodazole (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Key spindle parameters, such as its area and the amount and distribution of microtubules, were not significantly affected by 30 pM nocodazole.
source: Second, key spindle parameters, such as its area and the amount and distribution of microtubules, were not significantly affected (Figure 7A–D and 'Materials and methods').
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7A–D.

claim: With 25 pM taxol, the mean number of apical/basal astrals in neurogenic APs increased to 10.5 ± 0.6, similar to DMSO-only treated and untreated proliferating APs.
source: The extremely low taxol concentration of 25 pM increased the mean number of apical/basal astrals in neurogenic APs to 10.5 ± 0.6 (Figure 6H), similar to DMSO-only treated and untreated proliferating APs (Figure 6E, Figure 2H).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6H.

claim: In the presence of 25 pM taxol, the mean number of apical/basal astrals in APs overexpressing wt LGN increased to 12.3 ± 0.7, significantly higher than wt LGN-overexpressing APs incubated only with DMSO (9.9 ± 0.6).
source: Indeed, in the presence of 25 pM taxol, the mean number of apical/basal astrals in APs increased further to 12.3 ± 0.7, significantly higher than wt LGN-overexpressing APs incubated only with DMSO (9.9 ± 0.6) (Figure 6K).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6K.

claim: 25 pM taxol alone did not significantly decrease the amplitude of spindle orientation variability in either proliferating or neurogenic APs (DMSO proliferating 13.3 ± 1.7°, taxol proliferating 14.2 ± 1.6°, DMSO neurogenic 22.5 ± 2.7°, taxol neurogenic 20.4 ± 2.1°).
source: Interestingly, 25 pM taxol alone did not significantly decrease the amplitude of spindle orientation variability, neither in proliferating nor in neurogenic APs (Figure 8G; DMSO proliferating 13.3 ± 1.7°, taxol proliferating 14.2 ± 1.6°, DMSO neurogenic 22.5 ± 2.7°, taxol neurogenic 20.4 ± 2.1°).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: In mixed APs overexpressing LGN-wt and treated with taxol, spindle orientation variability decreased to a level (15.1 ± 2.3°) similar to control, non-LGN-overexpressing proliferating APs.
source: In this population of mixed APs (Figure 8E–F, Videos 8,9), spindle orientation variability decreased to a level (15.1 ± 2.3°) similar to control, non-LGN-overexpressing proliferating APs (Figure 8G).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8G.

claim: Incubation with 30 pM nocodazole was sufficient to increase the amplitude of spindle orientation variability in proliferating APs to a level similar to control neurogenic APs (Control proliferating 13.1 ± 1.7°, nocodazole proliferating 23.8 ± 3.8°, Control neurogenic 22.7 ± 2.7°).
source: Interestingly, using live imaging of organotypic slice culture, incubation with 30 pM nocodazole was sufficient to increase the amplitude of spindle orientation variability in proliferating APs to a level similar to control neurogenic APs (Figure 9A–E; Videos 10–13; Control proliferating 13.1 ± 1.7°, nocodazole proliferating 23.8 ± 3.8°, Control neurogenic 22.7 ± 2.7°).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 9A–E.

claim: With 30 pM nocodazole, the proportion of asymmetric divisions in proliferating APs increased to a level similar to control neurogenic divisions (60% vs 62%).
source: However, with 30 pM nocodazole, the proportion of asymmetric divisions in proliferating APs increased to a level similar to control neurogenic divisions (Figure 9H, second and third bar, white = 60% vs 62%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 9H.

claim: 30 pM nocodazole is sufficient to induce mitotic proliferating APs to behave as neurogenic ones with respect to the number of apical/basal astrals, spindle orientation variability, and cell division symmetry.
source: Together, these data show that 30 pM nocodazole is sufficient to induce mitotic proliferating APs to behave as neurogenic ones with respect to the number of apical/basal astrals (Figure 6A–F), spindle orientation variability (Figure 9A–E), and cell division symmetry (Figure 9F–H).
evidence: The claim is inferred from multiple experimental results showing that 30 pM nocodazole recapitulates neurogenic AP characteristics.

claim: Incubation with 30 pM nocodazole for 24 hr resulted in a decrease in the proportion of APs (62.5 ± 1.8% vs 53.8 ± 0.7%).
source: Compared to the DMSO control, incubation with 30 pM nocodazole for 24 hr resulted in a decrease in the proportion of APs, as identified by being in the ventricular zone (VZ) and having a characteristic transcription factor expression pattern (Pax6-positive, Tbr2-negative; Figure 10A–C, 62.5 ± 1.8% vs 53.8 ± 0.7%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 10A–C.

claim: Incubation with 30 pM nocodazole for 24 hr resulted in a concomitant increase in the proportion of Tbr2-positive newborn BPs in the VZ (34.3 ± 2.1% vs 43.1 ± 2.4%).
source: Interestingly, a concomitant increase was observed in the proportion of Tbr2-positive newborn BPs in the VZ (Figure 10A–C, 34.3 ± 2.1% vs 43.1 ± 2.4%).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 10A–C.

claim: More mitoses were found in the SVZ with 30 pM nocodazole than in controls (1.96 ± 0.16 vs 1.32 ± 0.029).
source: Confirming this, more mitoses were found in the SVZ with 30 pM nocodazole than in controls (phosphorylated histone 3 (PH3) immunoreactivity; Figure 10D–F, 1.96 ± 0.16 vs 1.32 ± 0.029).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 10D–F.

claim: The total number of mitoses did not change significantly with minimal nocodazole when analysed by either PH3 (control: 7.98 ± 0.57, nocodazole: 8.22 ± 0.58) or by pVim (control: 7.80 ± 0.52, nocodazole: 8.09 ± 0.42).
source: Importantly, the total number of mitoses did not change significantly with minimal nocodazole when analysed by either PH3 (Figure 10F, control: 7.98 ± 0.57, nocodazole: 8.22 ± 0.58) or by pVim (Figure 10—figure supplement 1F, control: 7.80 ± 0.52, nocodazole: 8.09 ± 0.42).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 10F and Figure 10—figure supplement 1F.

claim: More neurons were found in the presence of 30 pM nocodazole than in the presence of only DMSO (381.2 ± 11.4 vs 327.2 ± 12.0).
source: Counting the number of cells positive for the neuronal marker Tbr1 confirmed this. More neurons were found in the presence of 30 pM nocodazole than in the presence of only DMSO (Figure 10G–I, 381.2 ± 11.4 vs 327.2 ± 12.0).
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 10G–I.

claim: An acute reduction in the number of apical/basal astrals that leads to an increase in asymmetric AP divisions can increase BPs and neurogenesis.
source: Together, these results show that an acute reduction in the number of apical/basal astrals that leads to an increase in asymmetric AP divisions can increase BPs and neurogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that reducing apical/basal astrals increases asymmetric divisions, BPs, and neurons.

claim: A distinct subpopulation of astrals, the apical/basal astrals, governs spindle orientation.
source: This shows that a distinct subpopulation of astrals, the apical/basal astrals, governs spindle orientation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that only apical/basal astrals, not central astrals, affect spindle orientation.

claim: The selective reduction in the number of apical/basal astrals by using minimal nocodazole mimics the reduction observed in vivo and increases the proportion of asymmetric AP divisions and the pool of BPs, ultimately leading to more neurogenesis.
source: Our selective reduction in the number of apical/basal astrals, by using minimal nocodazole, mimics the reduction observed in vivo and increases the proportion of asymmetric AP divisions and the pool of BPs, ultimately leading to more neurogenesis.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that minimal nocodazole treatment recapitulates in vivo changes and increases neurogenesis.

claim: The reduction in apical/basal astrals is the earliest change reported thus far in the cytoarchitecture of APs that switch from proliferation to neurogenesis.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this reduction is also the earliest change reported thus far in the cytoarchitecture of APs that switch from proliferation to neurogenesis.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with previous literature and the authors' knowledge of the field.

claim: As mammalian APs switch to neurogenesis, the spindle becomes less restricted to an orientation precisely perpendicular to the apico-basal axis as a result of fewer apical/basal astrals anchoring the spindle to the cell cortex.
source: We show that, as mammalian APs switch to neurogenesis, the spindle becomes less restricted to an orientation precisely perpendicular to the apico-basal axis (Sauer, 1935; Smart, 1972a, 1972b; Huttner and Brand, 1997) as a result of fewer apical/basal astrals anchoring the spindle to the cell cortex (Figure 10J).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The increase in BPs upon increasing spindle orientation variability by minimal nocodazole treatment is consistent with previous studies showing more BPs in mice where spindles were tilted by perturbing the LGN binding partner Inscuteable or LGN itself.
source: The increase in BPs upon increasing spindle orientation variability by minimal nocodazole treatment is consistent with previous studies showing more BPs in mice where spindles were tilted by perturbing the LGN binding partner Inscuteable (Postiglione et al., 2011), or LGN itself (Konno et al., 2008; Shitamukai et al., 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison with previous studies (Postiglione et al., 2011; Konno et al., 2008; Shitamukai et al., 2011).

claim: LGN is necessary for APs to have a normal number of apical/basal astrals.
source: Using an LGN KO mouse (Konno et al., 2008), LGN is now shown to be necessary for APs to have a normal number of apical/basal astrals.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from LGN KO mice.

claim: Lack of LGN did not affect the number of central astrals, corroborating that loss of apical/basal astrals is sufficient to increase spindle deviations and asymmetric divisions.
source: Importantly, lack of LGN did not affect the number of central astrals, corroborating that loss of apical/basal astrals is sufficient to increase spindle deviations and asymmetric divisions.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing selective effects of LGN loss on apical/basal astrals.

claim: LGN is required for maintaining symmetric AP divisions through cortical anchoring of apical/basal astrals.
source: Together, these data show that LGN is required for maintaining symmetric AP divisions through cortical anchoring of apical/basal astrals.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental results showing that LGN perturbation reduces apical/basal astrals and increases asymmetric divisions.

claim: When APs switched to neurogenesis, the enrichment of LGN at the basal cell cortex was largely reduced, and it was further reduced all around the cell cortex in BPs.
source: When APs switched to neurogenesis, the enrichment of LGN at the basal cell cortex was largely reduced, and it was further reduced all around the cell cortex in BPs.
evidence: The claim is supported by immunofluorescence data showing LGN distribution in different progenitor types.

claim: A spatially selective loss of cortical LGN could reduce cortical anchor points and lead to fewer astrals in specific regions of the cell cortex.
source: A spatially selective loss of cortical LGN could therefore reduce cortical anchor points and lead to fewer astrals in specific regions of the cell cortex (Figure 10J).
evidence: The claim is inferred from the correlation between LGN distribution and astral abundance.

claim: The altered cleavage plane orientation in Lis1-deficient APs could be due, at least in part, to a loss of apical/basal astrals.
source: The present findings suggest that the altered cleavage plane orientation in Lis1-deficient APs could be due, at least in part, to a loss of apical/basal astrals.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the current findings and previous studies on Lis1.

claim: The baseline number of remaining central astrals is required for the primary establishment and structural stability of a spindle.
source: An intriguing scenario is that this baseline number of remaining astrals is required for the primary establishment and structural stability of a spindle.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on inference from the observation that central astrals remain constant.
